title: Medically Refractory Multiple Sclerosis Is Successfully Treated with Plasmapheresis in a Super Morbidly Obese Pregnant Patient
case_prompt:
A 25-year-old G2P0 woman at 18 weeks’ gestation presented with bilateral lower extremity weakness and right flank pain. She has relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis diagnosed at age 17 and super morbid obesity (BMI 55). Fingolimod was discontinued 4 weeks before conception. Her pregnancy was complicated by threatened abortion and persistent vaginal bleeding, requiring bed rest. During her bed rest, she developed fever, right flank pain, and severe paraparesis requiring hospitalization.

Initial evaluation revealed pyelonephritis on urinalysis and urine culture. Noncontrast MRI of the brain and cervical spine showed a new extensive demyelinating lesion from C1 to C4. She received antibiotics and 6 days of IV methylprednisolone 1,000 mg daily, with moderate improvement, and was discharged to acute rehabilitation.

Three weeks later, she returned with right flank pain, generalized weakness after a fall, and tingling in her extremities. On examination, mental status was normal. Muscle tone was increased in the left upper and bilateral lower extremities. Motor testing demonstrated asymmetrical moderate-to-severe tetraparesis worse distally, with generalized hyperreflexia, bilateral clonus, and bilateral Babinski signs. Sensation to light touch, pinprick, and vibration was decreased without a clear sensory level. Urinalysis again indicated a urinary tract infection, and MRI of the head demonstrated progression of T2 hyperintense signal abnormality in the craniocervical cord. Vitamin B12 and ACE levels were normal, and serum aquaporin-4 antibodies were negative. She was restarted on IV methylprednisolone 250 mg every 6 hours. After 5 days, she showed minimal motor improvement.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Rebound demyelination due to fingolimod withdrawal — “these rebound relapses can be steroid resistant and occur despite the usual protective hormonal influence of early pregnancy…”  
2. Neuromyelitis optica — “to rule out a possible diagnosis of neuromyelitis optica, an aquaporin 4 AQR4 antibody was tested and was negative.”  
3. Vitamin B12 deficiency — “vitamin B12 … were checked and were within normal limits.”  
4. Neurosarcoidosis — “ACE levels were checked and were within normal limits.”
